1.pericope_label: Job answered and said, How long will ye vex my soul, and break me in pieces with words? These ten times have ye reproached me: ye are not ashamed that ye make yourselves strange to me. And be it indeed that I have erred, mine error remaineth with myself. If indeed ye will magnify yourselves against me, and plead my reproach against me

schools.summary: Gill opens on the pause, Bildad being heard out without interruption before Job rose in his own defence; he makes the vexation of the soul the sting, since to be vexed to the heart is worse than any bodily vexation, and catalogues what galls a godly man, the corruptions that are as thorns in his side, the fiery darts of temptation and the talk of the profane that wearied righteous Lot, ending where Job stands, galled by his own companions. On the number he canvasses and rejects the arithmeticians, Jarchi's ten paragraphs, Saadiah's pairing of speech with answer and the five orations each carrying a doubled slight, preferring Aben Ezra that no tally is intended; he notes that to be reproached for righteousness' sake is the common lot and that Moses reckoned such reproach greater riches than the treasures of Egypt, but that to be reproached by friends as a hypocrite is cutting. He will not have the concession taken for a confession, though he allows a stumble in judgment, practice or speech, since who can understand his errors and none is to be made an offender for a word; and he closes on the swagger they are warned against, talking big and opening the mouth wide with swelling words.

Henry notices where the answer begins, Bildad having twice led with a How long, so that Job replies in kind and with the better warrant, a stronger case being shown for defending ourselves, right being on our side, than for assaulting a brother. He itemises the injury under six heads: they wounded his spirit, broke him in pieces with words, charged him with what he knew not, stood aloof in his trouble, grew big to make him small, which he calls a mean thing, trampling those already down, and worst of all pleaded his calamity against his uprightness where they should have pleaded his uprightness against his calamity, asking where an honest man shall be found if a bad name counts as evidence. On the number he agrees that it means often, yet turns it back on the speaker, since to keep so exact a reckoning looks like a design of retaliation and we serve our own peace better by letting injuries drop than by scoring them up; and he hears in the clause about error a disclaimer of teaching, the mistake kept at home and pressed on nobody else, which is the one thing that makes error tolerable.

Clarke is blunt about the three: no kind word drops from them at any point, none of them being touched with tenderness, the term friend must here mean a cold-blooded acquaintance, and posterity has by common consent handed them down to endless infamy. He sends the reader to Genesis for the idiom of the ten times, and hears in the companion phrase a whole history of reversal, since in affluence they were his intimates and seemed glad of his happiness and now they barely know him, circumstances changing men's minds. On the concession he reads a plea for pity, the harm falling on the one who erred and no public stain lying on his life, and asks why a man should be treated as though his life had been one general blot and his example a public curse. Wesley gives the ten as a certain number put for an uncertain, charges them with carrying themselves like strangers and condemning him as though they had never known his integrity, and reads the error clause as deserving pity rather than reproach, since the sufferer smarts for his own sin.

Keil and Delitzsch call the opening a justified quousque tandem, a man in unutterable agony now racked by three assailants of united strength, and take the ten as round rather than exact. Ellicott marks the same mirroring of Bildad's own opening and names what provoked it, a personal malice infused into the last charges which the sufferer felt most keenly of all; he reads the error clause as a plea that the sufferer alone bears the consequence while his companions neither sympathise nor suffer with him.

debates.question: Is the count of ten reproaches to be taken strictly?

sides.position: no: it is a round number for many, on the analogy of the same idiom elsewhere in Scripture
no, and the keeping of such a reckoning is itself a fault, looking like a design of retaliation

debates.question: What does it mean that the error remains with himself?

sides.position: that he has not imposed it on anybody else, which is the one thing that makes an error tolerable
that he alone bears its consequence, so that it calls for pity rather than reproach

debates.question: How are the three to be characterised?

sides.position: cold-blooded acquaintances, untouched by tenderness and justly handed down to infamy
men governed by the spirit of the world, who grow strange to a friend in trouble and big against one who is down
friends who have infused a personal malice into their charges

outliers: Gill alone surveys and rejects the Jewish arithmetic of the ten reproaches, naming Jarchi, Saadiah and Aben Ezra, and settles for no tally at all.
Henry alone turns the complaint back on the complainer, finding the exact reckoning of injuries a peevish thing that serves our own peace badly.
themes: an answer that begins where the attack began
vexation reaching the soul and not the bones only
a number nobody will count strictly
an error kept at home

6.pericope_label: Know now that God hath overthrown me, and hath compassed me with his net. Behold, I cry out of wrong, but I am not heard: I cry aloud, but there is no judgment. He hath fenced up my way that I cannot pass, and he hath set darkness in my paths. He hath stripped me of my glory, and taken the crown from my head. He hath destroyed me on every side, and I am gone: and mine hope hath he removed like a tree. He hath also kindled his wrath against me, and he counteth me unto him as one of his enemies. His troops come together, and raise up their way against me, and encamp round about my tabernacle

schools.summary: Gill notes that Job has always ascribed his losses to God, whoever the instruments, and fences the second verb carefully, since God made him neither perverse in word nor crooked in act nor twisted his cause, so that Bildad's question whether the Almighty perverts justice gets a flat no. He hears the cry as a complaint of violence, raiders on the herds and Satan on the body, uttered as though in open court as a plain breach of justice. The blocked road he works as a traveller's image: the godly are pilgrims whose path, though rough, is commonly passable, sometimes hedged so that they brush through scratched and torn, but at times walled with hewn stone so that they halt, not knowing which way to turn. The glory stripped he reads in a civil sense only, the magistrate's robe, the substance and the household, expressly not the robe of Christ's righteousness; destruction on every side he takes as more than trouble on every side, the estate and the body demolished together; and the troops he makes God's own soldiers, coming at a word.

Henry sets the verses as three glances. Looking back, a hand has stripped him, and he adds one item the rest miss, the opportunity of doing good, reading the whole as worldly glory's vanity. Looking down, the besiegers are God's own troops, lying about his tent as soldiers invest a city, cutting off supply and battering without pause, where once that same encampment was a hedge of protection. Looking forward, the road is walled and dark, with none to say how long. He will not leave the uprooted tree bare: hope in this life perishes, but a good man's hope, cut off here, is only transplanted from the nursery to the garden of the Lord, moved from sand to rock. On the kindled wrath he asks what the fire of hell is but the wrath of God, and warns that seared consciences will feel it hereafter though they do not fear it now while enlightened consciences fear it now and shall not feel it hereafter; and he calls it a gross but common mistake to think that whom God afflicts he treats as enemies, since as many as he loves he rebukes and chastens.

Clarke draws the practical inference, that the matter lies between the sufferer and God, who commissioned nobody to add reproaches to his chastisements, and then turns the net into an antiquarian hunt: read backwards, the figure is a mode of combat, the Roman netman with his trident against the swordsman, flinging his mesh over the head so that a noose tightened at the neck, obliged if he missed to run the ground until he had gathered it again; he adds the Persian loop thrown over a horseman and the Goths' hooped pole-net, citing Olaus Magnus, and elsewhere suspects the elephant pit of the previous chapter or an invading army. He alone strings the seven verses into one campaign, from unprovoked invasion to the storming of the royal city and the escape with the skin of the teeth; he hears only the cry and its silence, injustice alleged and nobody coming to help; and he keeps the uprooted tree hopeless, its roots out of the ground. Wesley reads the cry of oppression by the three, lists the glory as estate, children, authority and comfort with the crown for power and honour laid in the dust, gives Henry's transplanting of the tree in almost the same words, and makes the troops God's soldiers marching under his conduct and casting up a trench.

Ellicott wants none of Clarke's machinery: Bildad had talked at length of the ungodly snared in his own sin, and Job answers that substance without borrowing the words, choosing a different term for net and laying the hand that holds it on God. He explains why the desolation is piled so high, the darker the forsaking the greater the worth of the confession now coming, this severity having driven the man nearer to God and not away, and counts the heaped figures, assault unredressed, walls all round, a hope torn up like the tree of an earlier chapter. Keil and Delitzsch, counting thirty lines between the cry and the plea for pity, keep that whole stretch together as one block of verse.

debates.question: What figure lies behind the net?

sides.position: an ancient mode of combat with net and trident, or the Persian noose, or the hooped net of the Goths
simply the hunter’s net, answering Bildad’s talk of the snared sinner with a word Bildad had not used

debates.question: Who has done the wrong that is cried against?

sides.position: the raiders who took the herds and the adversary who struck the body, a breach of justice cried as in open court
an unnamed injustice met with silence, nobody coming to help
the three friends, who oppress him
God, whose forsaking is set out at length to raise the worth of the coming confession

debates.question: What is the glory of which he was stripped?

sides.position: civil glory only, the robe and the substance and the household, and expressly not the robe of Christ’s righteousness
estate, children, authority and comfort, with the crown for power and honour
the same, with the opportunity of doing good added to the list

debates.question: How far does the military figure run?

sides.position: through the whole passage as one connected campaign in seven stages
not as a narrative but as three separate glances, backward, downward and forward
as one strophic block, the thirty lines between the cry and the plea for pity belonging together

outliers: Clarke alone leaves the text for an antiquarian excursus on net-fighting, citing the Roman arena, a Persian cavalry noose and Olaus Magnus on the Goths.
Keil and Delitzsch alone argue from line-counting, dividing the speech by the number of verse-lines rather than by its subject.
themes: a hand owned behind every loss
a net cast over the head
a road walled up and darkened
a hope uprooted and transplanted
a siege laid by God’s own troops

13.pericope_label: He hath put my brethren far from me, and mine acquaintance are verily estranged from me. My kinsfolk have failed, and my familiar friends have forgotten me. They that dwell in mine house, and my maids, count me for a stranger: I am an alien in their sight. I called my servant, and he gave me no answer; I intreated him with my mouth. My breath is strange to my wife, though I intreated for the children's sake of mine own body. Yea, young children despised me; I arose, and they spake against me. All my inward friends abhorred me: and they whom I loved are turned against me

schools.summary: Gill keeps the war figure of the preceding verses: as a besieger cuts the defenders off from their allies, so every quarter from which comfort might come is held away; and he adds that these brethren came at last and showed brotherly love then. The kinsfolk have not died but ceased, those once near in relation and often near in place ceasing to be near in affection. He cares less for the moral than for the household, holding that the dwellers in the house are not neighbours, as the Septuagint has it, nor tenants, but strangers taken in and given food and raiment as the law requires, or else proselytes, and he passes on Jerome's tradition that the house stood at Carnea beyond Jordan. On the wife he offers a corrupt breath and then withdraws it shrewdly, since were the smell so bad the three could not have sat in the room through these long speeches, and prefers either his talk, unwelcome since he met her counsel to curse God by telling her she spoke like a foolish woman, or his very life, which wearied her. The mocking children he places out of doors, repeating what their parents taught; and the men of his secret he makes those to whom the heart and the most private affairs were committed, every one of whom now withholds respect.

Henry divides the question of agency: God laid on the affliction that frightened the kindred away and ordered their coldness toward the completing of the trial, but the coldness was their own sin and Satan's work, since he alienates men from a brother in trouble, and though every creature is to us what God makes it, that excuses nobody's ingratitude. He sharpens the servants' refusal from the master's side, since Job never despised their cause when they pleaded and now they despise his, and since, sick as he was, he did not turn imperious but entreated where he might have commanded, so that we should not wonder to get evil from those we have deserved well of. The familiar friends he says had heard of the trouble and designed a visit and simply forgot it, while the inward friends kept as far off as they could because he was poor and could not entertain them and because he was a loathsome spectacle, which shows how uncertain the friendship of men is and that adversity is the proof of friendship. The wife's estrangement he makes the price of his refusing her counsel, and the mocking children he places indoors, the offspring of his own servants and his servants by birth, who neither feared nor loved him when he rose to check them.

Clarke reads the passage as a study in lost fortune, reverenced once by all and esteemed now by none, many worshipping a rising sun who think little of one gone down, and some being reproached with the eminence they lost though not to blame for losing it; he illustrates it with a bishop driven from his see under Queen Mary and never restored, greeted one morning with a pun on his title and answering in kind. The kinsfolk he renders literally as departed, gone from the house now that there is no more hope of gain. On the clause about the children he keeps the sense literal and infers surviving younger children, too small for the feast where the rest died, rejecting the Septuagint's concubines as unsupported by the Hebrew and quoting Coverdale instead; and the inward friends he glosses simply as the greatest intimates. Wesley states the rule of agency in a line, that we are to look for the hand of God in the slights of friends as in the injuries of enemies, observes that the maids are named because women commonly have the more compassionate hearts, and explains the rising of the last verse as rising from his seat to show respect to inferiors.

Keil and Delitzsch weigh the servant's silence by setting past against present, one who once read every order in his master's eyes and waited on his nod now neither coming at the call nor troubling to answer; and on the men of his counsel they work the Hebrew for a secret back to roots meaning to speak close or to be made impenetrable, so that the phrase names those trusted with the most private plans. They add, alone, that the clause about the loved turning against him is aimed at the three sitting before him. Ellicott keeps the inward friends general, the men of his counsel familiar with his affairs, repoints the clause about the children out of the quarrel altogether so that it speaks of Job's own kindness toward the children of his mother's womb, that is his brethren, and lifts the whole lament off its speaker, finding a verse of the Psalter copied from it and hearing throughout the accents of the Man of sorrows, in whom these words, and David's and Jeremiah's, are at home.

debates.question: Whose doing is the desertion?

sides.position: God's, who holds off every source of comfort as a besieger cuts off allies
God's in the affliction that frightened them, Satan's and their own in the coldness itself
God's hand is to be looked for in the slights of friends as in the injuries of enemies

debates.question: What has become strange to his wife?

sides.position: not his literal breath, which the three could not have borne in the room, but his talk or his very life
he himself, since he would not take her counsel to curse God and die
the clause belongs elsewhere: it speaks of his own kindness toward his brethren
the clause is literal, and implies younger children still living who had missed the fatal feast

debates.question: Where are the children who mock him?

sides.position: out of doors, repeating what their parents had taught them
inside the house: the servants’ offspring, his own servants by birth

debates.question: Who are those whom he loved that have turned against him?

sides.position: the three friends sitting in front of him
his intimates and confidants generally, the men familiar with his private affairs

outliers: Ellicott alone reads the lament typologically, finding a Psalm copied from it and hearing in it the accents of the Man of sorrows.
Clarke alone illustrates the verse from Tudor England, with the deprived bishop who answered a jest about his lost title in the same Latin coin.
Gill alone locates the house itself, passing on Jerome's tradition that it stood at Carnea beyond Jordan.
themes: a circle of desertion drawn from outside in
a servant who will not answer
a wife who will not come near
contempt learned by children
the men of his secret turned enemies

20.pericope_label: My bone cleaveth to my skin and to my flesh, and I am escaped with the skin of my teeth. Have pity upon me, have pity upon me, O ye my friends; for the hand of God hath touched me. Why do ye persecute me as God, and are not satisfied with my flesh? Oh that my words were now written! oh that they were printed in a book! That they were graven with an iron pen and lead in the rock for ever!

schools.summary: Gill observes the reversal of the body, the bones having once cleaved to the flesh and now, the flesh being wasted, cleaving to the skin and showing through it, disease and grief between them leaving little else. On the rebuke he makes it a question of standing: the Almighty answers to none, which men do, so his dealings are no precedent for ours, and we are bound to be merciful as he is merciful and not licensed to harry his people because he has harried them for his own ends; he hunted Job as a lion hunts, which gave the three no warrant to join in, and Gill notes a second rendering where the clause asks why they hound him like one of the wicked lately described. On the wish he holds that what is to be recorded is not the apology already made but the confession about to come, since what is written abides while what is only spoken is soon forgotten; and on the lead he argues for an iron stile writing on a leaden sheet, lead leaving no lasting mark of its own and none at all on stone, while reporting Jarchi's alternative of letters chiselled into rock with molten lead run into the grooves.

Henry marks the abruptness of the turn and its reason: the man turns from grieving to triumphing, for others' edification as much as his own comfort, since those at hand would heed little and he wanted this kept for later generations. He has him disown his earlier outbursts as unadvised words he would rather see forgotten, and mark what comes next as deliberate, to be set in characters a runner could read, bound into a book rather than loose papers, or cut into a monument with all the engraver's art. The wish was granted, he adds, the words standing in God's own book and told for a memorial wherever it is read. On the plea for pity he presses that it becomes friends to pity one another in trouble and not to shut up the bowels of compassion, and on the persecution that God gives account of none of his matters while we must give account of ours, so that we are to aim at being like the most holy and most merciful and not like the most high and most mighty.

Clarke takes the phrase about the teeth for a proverb of the narrowest escape, no thicker than the enamel, and says plainly it is a wonder the man lives. He asks whether what is sent is not already as much as a man can carry, and answers out of an English martyr's mouth at the stake, when a bystander flung a brand and split his face: why add this wrong? What the three assail is the spirit, the earlier blow having struck the body. He then turns the wish into a lecture on the history of writing, beginning with a correction of the translators, since the verb means traced or described and not printed, printing being two thousand years off; three methods are in view, a roll of papyrus or linen, one such drawn from an Egyptian mummy before his own eyes, an iron stile on lead sheets, and letters cut in rock, many surviving in Arabia. Wesley makes the usurpation twofold, a claim to omniscience that searches a heart for hypocrisy and a claim to the sovereign right of doing as one pleases, and gives the appetite in the next clause its teeth, likening them to beasts that will not devour prey without breaking the bones; he locates the touch that drew the cry in the spirit and not the flesh, displeasure being the heaviest calamity of all, and states Jarchi's practice of filling chiselled letters with lead as plain fact.

Keil and Delitzsch hear the change of register, strength and voice growing fainter and sadness replacing protest, so that the address takes a tone of importunate entreaty meant, if anything can, to reach their hearts, and they note that the three are his friends after all and that the pronoun is emphatic. Ellicott calls it an exceeding great and bitter cry, the second of its kind in these speeches, and agrees that what is to be written is the confession about to come, resting the point on the plain weight of the three verses following and perhaps on the word now; he adds that the wish for printing points to a primitive time when writing involved more or less of engraving.

debates.question: How do the iron pen and the lead go together?

sides.position: an iron stile writing upon a sheet of lead, since lead leaves no lasting mark of its own
letters chiselled into rock with molten lead run into the grooves to keep them legible, which Gill reports from Jarchi

debates.question: What is wrong with persecuting him as God does?

sides.position: it usurps a sovereignty that answers to nobody, which no man holds
it claims both an omniscience that can find hypocrisy in a heart and a right to do as one pleases with a man
it adds a second wound where the first was already more than could be borne
we are to imitate God in mercy and not in sovereignty, since he gives account of none of his matters and we must give account of ours

outliers: Clarke alone turns the verse into a history of writing materials, dating the invention of printing and listing papyrus, lead sheets and rock-cut inscriptions.
Keil and Delitzsch alone read the plea as a change of register, hearing the voice itself grow weaker where the others hear only a change of subject.
themes: a body reduced to skin and bone
a narrow escape become a proverb
a plea for pity twice repeated
an office usurped
a wish for words that will outlast him

25.pericope_label: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: and though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another; though my reins be consumed within me

schools.summary: Gill settles the grammar first, since the opening particle is neither but nor for but nearer namely, so that these three verses are precisely what the preceding wish asked to have cut into rock, and he cites Broughton's rendering to the same effect. He arrives at the identity of the Redeemer by elimination, barring any human vindicator, since no man stands upon the earth at the latter day, and barring the Father, who is seldom given that title and never stood here, so that the Son of God is left. On the skin he makes the destruction the grave's work rather than the ulcers', the frame stripped at last of its flesh and its bones alike, and insists that the assurance of rising stands notwithstanding; and on the seeing he takes it for pleasure and profit, to the sufferer's inexpressible joy and satisfaction.

Henry calls these the weightiest lines in all the conferences and treats them as Job's creed, taught of God to believe in a living Redeemer and to look for the resurrection of the dead; he observes that after this we meet no more of the passionate and peevish complaining heard earlier, the hope having stilled the storm and cast anchor within the veil. He rehearses the kinsman's office, the heavenly inheritance mortgaged by sin and redeemed by one near of kin who paid the debt and made a new settlement, and presses that a living Redeemer saves to the uttermost since we are dying and he liveth. He handles the body's decay with a holy carelessness, pointing at his own wasted limbs and expecting them shortly to be a feast for worms, and says the glory of the rising shines the brighter for it, the power that made a body of common dust being able to raise it from its own; soul and body shall come together again and Job and God shall come together again, the sight being had with eyes of flesh and by no proxy, and the last clause he reads as every desire summed up and concluded in this one.

Clarke calls the passage the most disputed in the book, more having been written on it than would fill the whole of Job printed in capitals, and lays down a premise neither party can do without, that the speaker is under special inspiration and prophesying, since no man of that age could speak unaided of a rising from the dead and his restoration was equally improbable. Weighing which revelation God would rather give, he takes the greater, a doctrine fit to govern wayward passions deserving so solemn a disclosure where news the three would shortly witness anyway did not. He restricts the title of Redeemer to one of the same kindred, born of a woman, glosses the verbs as a firm persuasion, a living One holding the keys of death, and an arising to give sentence, and renders the last two words over the dust, the dead being those reduced to it; on the skin he makes disease the destroyer and its object no body but a wretched composition of misery, and offers as an alternative a seeing of God in the flesh of the Kinsman who shall partake of ours. Wesley grounds the confidence in a living and powerful Redeemer who will plead his cause, rehearses the same kinsman's office of buying back a mortgaged estate and avenging a death and keeping a name alive, notes that no despairing speech is heard afterwards, and has the Redeemer standing upon the grave as a conquered enemy put beneath his feet.

Ellicott counts the earlier speeches that wanted a daysman, a witness in the heavens, an advocate and a surety, and finds the sufferer now past wanting, since God will take those offices himself and the Goel is a reality already, however future his appearing; Bildad had threatened him with the extinction of his memory, and he appeals instead to later ages, which Ellicott says we who still argue the sentence are the proof of. He is careful about the doctrine: the verses may not teach the resurrection directly, yet they express the faith for which a resurrection is the only natural justification, a living trust in a personal God who cannot leave his holy one in corruption, and a man may hold an opinion about rising and not believe in God, where Job did the reverse. He keeps the last two words strictly literal, upon dust, citing the identical idiom in the chapter on leviathan against the version over the dust, allows the clause about the skin to refer first to a present sight of God held against the corruption already at work, and notes where the Church has set the confession, at the head of the office for burying the dead. Keil and Delitzsch rule out the rival reading, finding in this speech no hope of bodily recovery at all, and render the clause as a seeing of God without flesh.

debates.question: Is the hope here a resurrection, or a restoration in this life?

sides.position: a resurrection and a Redeemer, plainly, and the turning point of the whole book
a resurrection, decided only after weighing which revelation God would more likely give
not the doctrine directly, but the faith for which a resurrection is the only natural justification
certainly not a bodily recovery: no such hope is expressed in this speech

debates.question: What do the words rendered upon the earth mean?

sides.position: upon dust, strictly, the same idiom being used unambiguously elsewhere in this book
over the dust, that is over the dead, above those who sleep in it and are to be raised
upon the grave, or upon death, as a conquered enemy put beneath his feet
upon the dust to which this earth will itself be reduced

debates.question: Who is the Redeemer?

sides.position: the Son of God, reached by barring both a human vindicator and the Father
Christ, as the kinsman with the legal right of redemption, born of a woman and of our flesh
God himself, taking upon him for Job the several offices of the next of kin

debates.question: Is God seen in the flesh or without it?

sides.position: in the flesh, with bodily eyes, the same body raised and glorified
without the flesh
perhaps first in this present life, a sight of God held against the corruption already at work
in the flesh of the Kinsman, who shall partake of ours in order to ransom the lost inheritance

outliers: Clarke alone argues the question by asking which of two possible revelations would do the most good in the world, and decides the point on that ground before touching the Hebrew.
Ellicott alone traces the confession through the earlier speeches as the last step in a series of wants, and alone notes its place at the head of the burial office.
themes: a creed cut into rock
a kinsman with the right to redeem
a Redeemer who is living now
a standing-place read four ways
a sight had by no proxy

28.pericope_label: But ye should say, Why persecute we him, seeing the root of the matter is found in me? Be ye afraid of the sword: for wrath bringeth the punishments of the sword, that ye may know there is a judgment

schools.summary: Gill states the purpose simply: having said what he believes, the sufferer tells the three what use they ought to make of it and what they should be saying to themselves and one another. On the sword he excludes the magistrate and the invader from the primary sense, leaving the avenging edge of divine justice, lest God whet the glittering blade of his justice and his hand take hold of judgment to requite the wrongs of the innocent, though he allows that human instruments may serve that end.

Henry takes the verse as a word of caution before it is a word of terror, telling the three what they should say in order to reduce themselves to a better temper, and he quotes the clause in the third person. He makes the thing found a living, quickening, commanding principle of grace in the heart, as needful to religion as a root is to a tree, which owes to it both its fixedness and its fruit, with love to God and to a brother, faith in Christ and a hatred of sin for its substance and all else leaves beside; serious godliness, he says, is the one thing needful. Then he turns it into a rule of charity: each is to see the principle rooted in himself, and to believe that many hold it who are not in everything of his mind and who have their follies and weaknesses and mistakes, and it is at his peril if he troubles such a man, since Job and the three differed over the methods of providence and agreed in believing another world. The terror he draws from the second coming, dreadful to those found smiting their fellow servants, warning that a censorious temper breeds the kind of crime that brings men under the magistrate and that God often avenges it himself, since those who showed no mercy shall find none; and he presses that there is not only a government now but a reckoning later, in which hard speeches must be answered for.

Clarke prefers a future to a conditional, then ye shall say, and borrows a sharper version of the question from Good in which the three stand already convinced of their fault. Against the received first person he sets the third, the reading of more than a hundred manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi and of several versions, which turns the clause from a confession into a verdict passed on Job by his accusers. The thing found he describes as a pure practice and a sound hope standing on a sound faith received from God himself. On the warning he is plain, that the anger they displayed is a thing God will resent and punish, and from the closing words he draws a proof rather than a threat, reasoning that the unequal division of wealth and want and of health and sickness in this life is itself evidence that a reckoning must come in which evil is punished and virtue rewarded; and he adds, for the vindication reading he had already declined, that a hope full of immortality sits awkwardly with a man who has cursed the day of his birth. Wesley keeps the sword general, some considerable judgment so called as in the song of Moses, takes the warning as kindly meant and given in time to be prevented, compresses the matter found into a phrase, that all true religion begins in living faith, and says of the last clause that God observes and will judge all their words and actions.

Ellicott puts the fork in the disputed phrase plainly, that it means either the cause of the suffering or the substance of godliness, and takes the first, reading the sentence as the three arguing backwards from the calamity, since God would strike no man without cause and therefore the cause must lie in this one; he notes the irony of the closing threat, that the punishment held over them is the very one of which they had taken this man for a conspicuous instance.

debates.question: What is the root of the matter?

sides.position: the cause of the suffering, which the three reason backwards to and locate in Job himself
a living, commanding principle of grace in the heart, as needful to religion as a root to a tree
living faith, in which all true religion begins
a pure practice and a sound hope resting on a sound faith received from God

debates.question: Is it found in me or in him?

sides.position: in him: the reading of over a hundred collated manuscripts and several versions, making the clause a verdict of his accusers
in me, as the received text has it

debates.question: Whose sword are they to fear?

sides.position: the avenging sword of divine justice, not the magistrate’s or the invader’s, though these may be its instruments
both: a censorious temper breeds crimes that bring men under the magistrate, and God often avenges it himself
some considerable judgment, called a sword as in the song of Moses
God’s judgments upon the anger they have displayed

debates.question: What does the closing clause about a judgment establish?

sides.position: that a future judgment must exist, since reward and affliction are so unequally divided in this life
that there is not only a present government but a reckoning in which hard speeches must be answered for
that God observes and will judge all their words and actions

outliers: Clarke alone rests the doctrine of a judgment on an argument from the unequal distribution of good and ill in the present life.
Henry alone turns the disputed phrase into a rule of forbearance, that men who differ about providence while agreeing about another world have no business harrying one another.
themes: a confession turned into counsel
a textual variant that changes the speaker
a root taken for piety or for guilt
a sword held over the accusers
a judgment still to come
